The WSJ article also omits other critical parts of Friedman's analysis of HR 676:

  • HR 676 would have completely removed all current state/local funding for Medicare and other programs. If that funding was kept and applied to universal healthcare, it would close the gap by $2.8T over the 10 year period.
  • Universal healthcare would remove the need for private healthcare for local/state/federal government employees (the employer paid premiums for government employees), a savings of $1.9T not included in WSJ's $15T number (admittedly this is conflating local/state with federal, but it is not inconceivable that the federal government could require local/state to pass the savings on to them or else they could increase federal income tax rates by the amount local/state sales/income taxes would decrease).
  • Employer and employee contributions towards employer-sponsored insurance are not considered part of income and are currently tax-free. Since universal healthcare would effectively eliminate this subsidy, Friedman predicts the government would save an additional $2.1T over 10 years. Add some other similar subsidies that would be eliminated (medical savings accounts, medical expense deductions, etc.) and this number goes up to $2.6T.

If you add all three of those up, you get another $7.3T in savings/revenue that WSJ failed to account for. With the $6.5T in tax hikes Sanders is proposing, that puts us at $13.8T of the $18T total for universal healthcare plus other proposals, which is definitely a lot closer.
